page: Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an instance in the Optimized Cloud Compute family. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs powered by an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz, configured with 1 physical core and 2 threads. The system includes 16.0 GB of system memory, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Storage is provided via a 320 GB local NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The CPU architecture is x86_64, supporting instruction sets such as AVX-512 (including AVX512F, AVX512_VNNI, and AVX512_BF16), AES cryptography, and AMD SVM virtualization.

Benchmark data reveals a contrast between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The single-core CPU performance measured via stress-ng is in the top tier (top 10%), and single-threaded compression tasks show strong performance, with gzip compression and bzip3 decompression both ranking in the top 25%. However, multi-core CPU performance under stress-ng falls into the average category, while the overall PassMark CPU score, extended instructions, encryption, and physics tests are positioned in the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth for large blocks is average, but small-block cached read bandwidth is weak.

Database and web serving benchmarks indicate specific limitations. Redis SET operations and PassMark database operations both rank in the bottom 25%, while static web serving throughput is in the bottom 10%. LLM inference speeds are also modest, with text generation on a 7B model performing in the bottom 10%. Given these performance characteristics, this instance is best suited for memory-intensive workloads that do not require high parallel processing power or extreme database transaction rates, such as lightweight caching layers, single-threaded data processing, or memory-heavy utility applications.
description: The Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an x86_64 server within the Optimized Cloud Compute family, featuring 2 dedicated vCPUs from an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz, 16.0 GB of RAM, and a 320 GB NVMe SSD. While single-core CPU performance is highly competitive, ranking in the top 10% on stress-ng benchmarks, multi-core performance and overall PassMark CPU scores fall into lower tiers. Memory read/write bandwidth for large blocks remains average, but database operations, Redis throughput, and static web serving show weaker results. This hardware profile, offering a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core alongside dedicated CPU resources, is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-heavy, single-threaded applications, lightweight caching, and basic file processing tasks rather than high-throughput web serving or intensive database workloads.
